migrationNotes: Spine: a school's pupil list points at a club list by number, and the same lookup is followed for the shop's orders, counted, narrowed to the customers who ordered, widened to every pair and finally checked against a condition that follows the wrong numbers.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): sql-join-matching-rows-8 (a pupil with club 2 matches one club). It is taught on the first and third screens.

lesson.title: Follow a relationship between tables

steps.headline: Looking up a number in another table

lead.text: A table stores each fact once. The shop's orders table records who placed an order with a customer_id, a number that is also the id of one row in the customers table. The customer's name lives only in the customers table, in the way a club's name lived only in the clubs list.

A join follows those numbers for you. JOIN customers ON customers.id = orders.customer_id pairs each order with the customer whose id equals the order's customer_id, and each pair becomes a single row holding columns from both tables. The ON condition says which values must be equal for two rows to belong together. A join that keeps only the pairs that satisfy the condition is an INNER JOIN, and a bare JOIN means the same thing.

The pupils and clubs show the same move on a small scale. If a pupil's club number is 2 and club 2 is the Choir, the pupil and the club become one row. The query makes that pairing for every pupil in a single step.
Do by hand what a join does: follow each pupil's club number to the club it names.

A join produces one result row for every pair of rows that satisfy the ON condition, and that fact explains how many rows come back. Take the pupils and the clubs. Each pupil has one club number and pairs with exactly one club, so four pupils make four pairs.

The clubs show the same thing from the other side. Chess has two pupils, so Chess appears in two rows. Choir and Drama have one pupil each. Art has none, and a club with no pupil never satisfies the condition, so it appears in no row at all. An inner join drops a row that has no partner.

afterFigure.text: Both queries in the picture return four rows, but the second starts from the clubs. A name repeats when its row has several partners, so Chess is listed twice. A name vanishes when its row has none, as Art does. Neither is a fault in the join. The result has one row for each matching pair, and its size follows the data.

queries.label: Pupils with their club
queries.sql: SELECT p.name AS pupil, c.name AS club FROM pupils AS p JOIN clubs AS c ON c.id = p.club ORDER BY p.id;

queries.label: Clubs with their pupils
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil FROM clubs AS c JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

lead.text: Orders refer to customers by number. Join the two tables on that number and think about how many matching pairs there are.

reveal.text: You counted matching pairs, not names. Each order matched the one customer it refers to, so the rows still stand for orders.

queries.label: Order references
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Names attached
queries.sql: SELECT o.id, c.name, o.amount FROM orders AS o JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id;

lead.text: A join gives one row for each order, so a question about customers needs one more step. To list the customers who have placed an order you join the tables and ask for the name, and each customer then appears once for every order. Writing SELECT DISTINCT before the name removes the repeats, as in the earlier lesson on different values.

afterFigure.text: The first query lists a name beside every order, six rows in all. The second keeps each name once and returns Ada, Ben and Cy. The customers table has four rows, and the result names only three of them. One customer is missing from the list, and the join is the reason.

queries.label: One row per match
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id;

queries.label: Customers who ordered
queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.name;

lead.text: One customer from the table, Dee, is missing from that list. Decide what the join did with that customer's row.

A join starts from the same raw material every time: every row of one table set beside every row of the other. The ON condition then throws away the pairs that don't belong together. If you leave the condition out, nothing is thrown away. CROSS JOIN is the form with no condition, and it returns every possible pair.

Take a lunch menu with two mains and three drinks. Pairing each main with each drink gives a row for every combination, 2 × 3 = 6. The count comes from multiplying the sizes of the two tables and not from adding them. A cross join is useful when you really do want every combination, as with a menu. It is also an easy way to produce a huge result by accident, because the row count grows with the product.

afterFigure.text: The picture lists the combinations and counts them. No value in one table has to relate to a value in the other. The pairs are there simply because the condition that would have removed them is missing.

queries.label: Every combination
queries.sql: SELECT m.item AS main, d.drink FROM mains AS m CROSS JOIN drinks AS d ORDER BY m.item, d.drink;

queries.label: Count the combinations
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS combinations FROM mains CROSS JOIN drinks;

lead.text: A cross join of the shop's customers and orders has no condition, so it pairs every customer with every order.

reveal.text: You paired each customer with each order. That is not the same as the orders each customer placed.

queries.label: Match the reference
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

queries.label: Every possible pair
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c CROSS JOIN orders AS o ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

steps.headline: A condition that follows the number

lead.text: The ON condition is where a join can go wrong without anyone noticing. SQL accepts any condition that compares two values, whether or not the values mean the same thing. A condition that follows the stored reference pairs the right rows. A condition that compares two columns which happen to hold similar numbers pairs the wrong ones, and the query still runs.

In the school lists, a pupil's club column holds the number of a club, so p.club = c.id follows the reference. Each pupil also has an id of their own, and p.id = c.id compares a pupil's id with a club's id. Both columns hold small numbers, so the second query does return rows. Some of them are wrong.

afterFigure.text: The first query gives the true pairs. The second pairs Cy with Drama and Di with Art, because their ids happen to equal those clubs' numbers, and neither pupil is really in that club. Ann and Bo come out right by luck. A join condition should compare the column that stores the reference with the key it refers to.

queries.label: Follow the club number
queries.sql: SELECT p.name AS pupil, c.name AS club FROM pupils AS p JOIN clubs AS c ON c.id = p.club ORDER BY p.id;

queries.label: Compare the ids
queries.sql: SELECT p.name AS pupil, c.name AS club FROM pupils AS p JOIN clubs AS c ON c.id = p.id ORDER BY p.id;

lead.text: In the shop, each order stores the number of its customer and each customer has an id of their own. Pick the condition that follows that reference.

lesson.orientation: Join keys deliberately and account for every matching pair.
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A school keeps two lists. The first has the pupils, and beside each name is a club number: Ann 1, Bo 2, Cy 1 and Di 3. The second has the clubs and says which number belongs to which club. Club 1, for example, is Chess.

Suppose someone asks who is in the chess club. You find Chess in the clubs list and read its number. Then you go down the pupil list looking for that number. Neither list had to carry the other's information. A number in one list pointed at a line in the other, and following the number was enough.

Databases keep their tables apart in exactly this way, so a question about customers and their orders means following numbers from one table to another. This lesson shows how a query follows the numbers for every row at once, how to tell how many rows will come back, and what happens to a row whose number points at nothing.

intro.promise: By the end you'll join two tables on their key and say how many rows to expect.

recap.keyIdea: A join pairs each row with the rows of another table whose key matches. A row with several matches repeats, and a row with none disappears from an INNER JOIN.

blocks.text: You found 2 pupils in Chess by following a club number, then counted 6 matching pairs between the shop's customers and orders. A cross join of the same tables gave 4 × 6 = 24 pairs.

recap.nextHook: An INNER JOIN drops Dee because she has no orders, and sometimes a report has to show her anyway. A librarian faces the same thing with a borrowing list: a pupil who has borrowed nothing still belongs on the list.

questions.prompt: How many rows does the INNER JOIN of customers and orders on customer_id return?
hints: Count matches, not different names.
Ada, Ben and Cy each contribute two order matches.
Ada, Ben and Cy each have two matches; Dee contributes none to an inner join.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the six orders references one existing customer, so there are six matching pairs.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Ada, Ben and Cy each have two matching orders. Dee has none, so no pair holds her.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the different names. Count matching pairs instead.
That pairs every customer with every order. A join on the key pairs only matches.

questions.prompt: Why is Dee absent from the INNER JOIN result?
hints: An inner join requires a match.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An INNER JOIN retains only matching pairs. Dee has no matching order in this dataset, so her customer row contributes no result row.

choices.label: INNER JOIN keeps only the first customer

questions.onCorrect: She has no matching order. An inner join keeps only pairs that match.

misconceptions.feedback: Names do not affect matching. The key values do.
INNER JOIN keeps every pair that matches, not just one customer.

questions.prompt: How many pairs does CROSS JOIN produce for four customers and six orders?
hints: For each customer, include every order.
Multiply the table sizes.
Evaluate 4 × 6 for every possible customer-order pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Every customer pairs with every order: 4 × 6 = 24.

questions.onCorrect: 24. A cross join pairs every customer with every order: 4 × 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two table sizes. A cross join pairs each row with every row of the other table.
That is the number of matching pairs. A cross join pairs every customer with every order.

questions.prompt: Which condition follows the stored relationship between orders and customers?
hints: The order's customer_id refers to the customer's id.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: c.id = o.customer_id follows the customer reference stored on each order. Matching the two tables' unrelated id columns would connect the wrong records.

questions.onCorrect: c.id = o.customer_id. The order's customer_id holds the customer's key.

misconceptions.feedback: That compares a customer key with an order key. They are different things.
A name is not a stored reference to an item.

questions.prompt: Customers A, B and C have two, zero and one orders respectively. How many rows does their INNER JOIN return?
hints: An unmatched customer contributes no inner-join row.
Add the order matches.
Evaluate 2 + 0 + 1; each matching order contributes a row.
questions.onCorrect: 3. Each matching order is one row, and the customer with none adds nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts customers with orders. Each matching order is a row.

questions.prompt: Why can a customer's name repeat in a correctly joined result?
hints: A one-to-many relationship creates one row for each match.

acceptedIdeas: A person can match several orders
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each matching customer-and-order pair produces a result row. A customer with several orders appears several times without the join being wrong.

choices.label: A person can match several orders
JOIN always duplicates every row twice
Names cannot be selected in SQL

questions.onCorrect: A person can match several orders. Each match gives its own row, so the name repeats.

misconceptions.feedback: Rows repeat once per match, and that number depends on the data.
Names are columns like any other and can be selected.

questions.prompt: Each pupil has a club number: Ann 1, Bo 2, Cy 1 and Di 3. Club 1 is Chess. How many pupils would a Chess list show?
hints: Which column connects a pupil to a club?
Find the pupils whose club number is the Chess number.
Count those pupils, not the clubs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Club 1 is Chess. Ann and Cy both have club number 1, so the list shows two pupils.

questions.onCorrect: 2. You followed a number from one list to the other. A join pairs rows by following keys like that.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the club. The list is of pupils.
That counts every pupil. Only those with the Chess number belong.

questions.prompt: A pupil row holds club = 2. The club ids are 1, 2 and 3. How many club rows does that pupil match in a join on the club number?
hints: Which club id equals the pupil's club number?
Compare the number with each club id in turn.
How many of the club ids are the same number?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the club row whose id is 2 matches, so the pupil pairs with one club row.

questions.onCorrect: 1. A join pairs a row only with rows whose key value is equal to its own.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every club. The pupil matches only the club with its own number.

questions.prompt: Customers P, Q and R have 3, 1 and 0 orders. How many rows does SELECT DISTINCT name over their INNER JOIN return?
hints: Which customers appear in the joined result at all?
A customer with no orders has no pair.
DISTINCT keeps each name once.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: P and Q each have orders, so each appears. R has no pair. DISTINCT leaves two names.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Only customers with a match appear, and DISTINCT keeps each name once.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the matching pairs. DISTINCT keeps each name once.
A customer with no orders has no pair, so no name appears for them.
